analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax on large inheritances.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to repeal the estate tax, backed by 36 of 50 Senate Republicans, was referred to the Finance Committee and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Sen. John Thune introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act of 2021 on March 9, 2021. It would have eliminated the federal estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax — the taxes that apply when very large amounts of wealth pass at death or jump generations — while keeping the gift tax with some adjustments [S2][S3]. The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced [S5]. It never got a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or any further action of any kind before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5][S1]. The estate tax only applies to estates above a large exemption (about $11.7 million per person in 2021), so repeal would primarily benefit the heirs of the wealthiest few thousand estates each year, while the tax revenue they currently pay would disappear from the federal budget.
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of the largest estates. The federal estate tax only reaches estates worth more than the exemption amount (roughly $11.7 million per person and $23.4 million per married couple in 2021), so only a small fraction of the wealthiest households' deaths trigger any tax at all. Fully repealing it would let the largest fortunes pass to heirs untaxed, with the largest savings going to the very biggest estates. Estate lawyers, trust and wealth-management firms, and the professional advisers who help families structure inheritances would also gain from permanent repeal and the planning work around it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs of multimillion-dollar estates and wealth advisers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax for decedents dying and transfers made after enactment [S2][S3].
It keeps the gift tax in place but makes conforming amendments, including an inflation-adjusted rate schedule for taxable gifts [S2][S3].
Because the estate tax applies only above a high exemption threshold, the entire tax cut flows to the heirs of very large estates; smaller estates pay nothing today and would gain nothing.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes raise federal revenue paid by taxpayers as a whole; repealing them removes that revenue, which would have to be made up through other taxes, lower spending, or more borrowing. The cost is spread broadly while the benefit is concentrated in the largest estates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary taxpayers, through lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate a tax paid almost exclusively by multimillion-dollar estates, shrinking federal revenue at a time when other taxes or debt would have to cover the difference. Supporters of the bill did not include a replacement revenue source.

The strongest good-faith argument for repeal — that surviving spouses and children are sometimes forced to sell family farms or small businesses to pay the tax — applies mainly to estates above the exemption threshold, which the exemption has already grown to shield; critics note that outright repeal chiefly benefits the very largest fortunes rather than typical family operations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a permanent tax cut worth the most to the heirs of the largest estates; the cost is the lost federal revenue those estates currently pay, borne by everyone else. The bill offered nothing for the more than 99% of estates that already pay no estate tax, so it is hard to characterize as anything other than a transfer to the wealthiest families — even if one accepts that estate taxation can burden some family businesses, the high exemption already protects most of them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 9, 2021 and read twice, then referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action appears in the record after the referral; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S5][S1].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill was not carried over [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No law changed, so the estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax remained in force on the largest estates. Taxpayers generally came out ahead of where they would have been under repeal, since that revenue was not eliminated; the heirs of the largest estates, whose interest the bill served, did not get the tax cut, and wealth-advisory interests did not get the permanence they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers generally; the estate tax survived

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act of 2021 in the Senate on March 9, 2021.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.role: Chair of the Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the Finance Committee, to which the bill was referred, and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 36 cosponsors were Republicans (36 of 50 Senate Republicans); no Democrat or independent cosponsored, and the Democratic chair never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates (wealthiest households)
industries.note: The bill was written to eliminate the taxes their inheritances pay. Because it died, the estate tax on estates above the exemption continued to apply.

industries.industry: Estate planning, trust, and wealth management
industries.note: Repeal would have removed the estate-tax-driven demand for trusts, valuation planning, and insurance products. The industry's interest here runs against the broad taxpayer interest in keeping the revenue.
